profiles.title: John the Forerunner: Angel of the Desert
profiles.subject: Saints

overview.text: The Uffizi explains the winged Baptist as a messenger preparing Christ’s advent. The wings belong to the iconographic title Angel of the Desert; the explanation relates them to biblical prophecies of the messenger and forerunner.
overview.reason: Necessary concise account of a modern published explanation; full prose reproduction rights have not been established.

blocks.text: The selected icon is attributed to Prokopiy Chirin of the Stroganov school, dated to the 1620s, and identified with the Tretyakov Gallery. John stands with wings, a scroll, and a vessel; the artwork’s title identifies him as the Desert Angel.

sourceRefs.locator: File description and displayed historic reproduction

blocks.reason: Necessary English description of the selected historic artwork and its published object metadata; no new theological interpretation.

blocks.text: The museum traces the winged type’s popularity in Eastern Christianity to the thirteenth century. In the related Uffizi example, a severed head in a basin refers to John’s martyrdom, while smaller scenes show his birth and beheading. Those scenes are specific to that museum’s example.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of a modern published explanation; full prose reproduction rights have not been established.

blocks.text: Metropolitan Tikhon’s reflection names John Prophet, Forerunner, and Baptist and interprets him as the friend of the Bridegroom. This published Orthodox explanation concerns John’s ministry; the wings are an artistic expression of his messenger role.

sourceRefs.locator: Description, first paragraph, wings and heavenly messenger

blocks.text: As it is written in the prophets, Behold, I send my messenger before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee. The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
